questions.independent_answer: To record when bark was last harvested
questions.provided_answer: To record when bark was last harvested
questions.evidence: Paragraph 1: the trunk is marked with the final digit of the harvest year, helping workers identify when it was last stripped.
questions.relationship_or_option_eliminations: Amount removed is not recorded; species identification is not the stated purpose; the passage says the bark grows back.
questions.logic_and_explanation_note: The explanation eliminates yield, species and failed regrowth; retrieval is direct.

questions.evidence: Paragraph 3: the second crop is generally unsuitable for quality stoppers; the desired structure is usually obtained from the third and later crops.
questions.relationship_or_option_eliminations: A newly planted tree has no crop; the first is irregular and unsuitable; the second is still generally unsuitable.
questions.logic_and_explanation_note: The explanation identifies third and later crops and rejects first and second; the newly planted option is implicitly excluded by the stated roughly 25-year first-harvest threshold. An explicit sentence would improve completeness, but the answer and teaching point remain clear.

questions.evidence: Paragraph 2 requires at least nine years between harvests. The second harvest at 34 therefore permits a third no earlier than age 43.
questions.relationship_or_option_eliminations: 35 is only one year after the second harvest; 34 is the second harvest itself; 52 adds an extra nine-year interval.
questions.logic_and_explanation_note: The explanation correctly adds nine years to the second harvest and handles all three numerical traps.

questions.independent_answer: Repeated bark harvests require both careful technique and waiting.
questions.provided_answer: Repeated bark harvests require both careful technique and waiting.
questions.evidence: Paragraphs 1 and 3 describe careful cutting to preserve the living tree; paragraphs 2 and 3 describe the nine-year interval and crop sequence.
questions.relationship_or_option_eliminations: Trunk thickness alone is insufficient; first cork is unsuitable for quality stoppers; trees remain standing and bark regrows.
questions.logic_and_explanation_note: The main-idea explanation joins cutting skill, harvest interval and crop sequence and addresses all three alternatives.

questions.independent_answer: Colour is floated and arranged on the bath.
questions.provided_answer: Colour is floated and arranged on the bath.
questions.evidence: Paragraph 1: drops of colour are supported at the bath surface and guided with a comb or tool; paper is then laid onto the surface to pick up the pattern.
questions.relationship_or_option_eliminations: Placing a completed sheet in a book is a later use; removing gum is unstated; painting dried paper reverses the described sequence.
questions.logic_and_explanation_note: The explanation follows the colour-on-bath-to-paper sequence and dismisses each alternative.

questions.independent_answer: To show that marbling could complement written pages
questions.provided_answer: To show that marbling could complement written pages
questions.evidence: Paragraph 2: marbled colours frame rather than replace the calligraphy in a manuscript album.
questions.relationship_or_option_eliminations: The text expressly rejects replacement; it does not say all ebru patterns were combed; the example does not date suminagashi.
questions.logic_and_explanation_note: The explanation uses the calligraphic border as evidence of complementing text and rejects each wrong purpose.

questions.independent_answer: Regular parallel lines shaped in the floating colour
questions.provided_answer: Regular parallel lines shaped in the floating colour
questions.evidence: Paragraph 2 links a comb to a regular design and mentions combed lines; regular lines in floating colour are therefore strongest evidence of combing.
questions.relationship_or_option_eliminations: Concentric ink rings are linked to suminagashi; a gum bath says nothing about whether a comb was used; speckles framing calligraphy also do not establish comb use.
questions.logic_and_explanation_note: The explanation compares all three competing observations and correctly treats regular lines as strong, not conclusive, evidence of combing.

questions.independent_answer: They can share a broad method without sharing a precise recipe.
questions.provided_answer: They can share a broad method without sharing a precise recipe.
questions.evidence: Paragraph 3: shared uses do not prove the same recipe, and 'marbled' identifies a broad method but not the comb, liquid, or colours used.
questions.relationship_or_option_eliminations: The bath may use gum or carrageenan; uses extend beyond covers; more than one cultural tradition is identified.
questions.logic_and_explanation_note: The explanation uses the final paragraph's method-versus-recipe distinction and rejects each overgeneralisation.

questions.independent_answer: A difference between stored pond water and the falling sea
questions.provided_answer: A difference between stored pond water and the falling sea
questions.evidence: Paragraph 1: gates retain pond water while the outside sea falls, creating the height difference that drives the wheel.
questions.relationship_or_option_eliminations: Millstones are driven rather than pumping water; a constant river describes a different mill; waves do not strike the wheel directly.
questions.logic_and_explanation_note: The explanation correctly identifies the stored-water head and rejects stones, a continuous river and direct wave action.

questions.independent_answer: The outside sea must fall enough to give the stored water a useful height advantage.
questions.provided_answer: The outside sea must fall enough to give the stored water a useful height advantage.
questions.evidence: Paragraph 2: after filling, the mill waits for a useful difference between pond and sea levels.
questions.relationship_or_option_eliminations: The pond is already full, so another incoming tide is unnecessary; the wheel need not be covered by rising sea; releasing all water would consume the stored head.
questions.logic_and_explanation_note: The explanation explains why the sea must fall after filling and addresses each timing trap.

questions.independent_answer: That tidal water management and familiar milling machinery operated together
questions.provided_answer: That tidal water management and familiar milling machinery operated together
questions.evidence: Paragraph 3: at Totton and Eling, the dam and gates manage supply while the wheel and stones grind; much machinery resembles other watermills.
questions.relationship_or_option_eliminations: Common machinery is explicitly noted; the dam manages water rather than only serving as a bridge; no claim is made about identical millstones at every site.
questions.logic_and_explanation_note: The explanation connects dam and sluice gear to familiar wheel and stones; its alternatives are individually rejected.

questions.independent_answer: The difference in water levels can grow before the miller releases pond water.
questions.provided_answer: The difference in water levels can grow before the miller releases pond water.
questions.evidence: Paragraph 1: closed gates retain water while the outside sea falls; release occurs after a head has developed.
questions.relationship_or_option_eliminations: A closed sluice does not imply a turning wheel or constant speed; it prevents immediate emptying; later refilling remains possible.
questions.logic_and_explanation_note: The explanation draws the conditional head-growth inference without assuming wheel speed, emptying or blocked refilling.
